Well, hello, it’s very nice to meet you. Thank you for fitting me in. You know, it feels a bit silly to be sitting in a doctor's office for this, but what brings me in is that for the past year or so—maybe a little longer, but definitely the last twelve months—I just feel like I am always, always puttering. 

I mean, from the moment I wake up, I’m looking for something to do. I’m fixing things, like the other day I was in the kitchen trying to tighten the hinges on the corner cabinet with a butter knife because I couldn't find my screwdriver, or I'm arranging things... I completely reorganized my linen closet by color and thread count just yesterday, and I had already done it back in the spring! And it’s not just around the house, either. I keep volunteering for just one more thing. The library book sale, the church committee, you name it, I raise my hand for it, even when my schedule is completely full. 

My friends tell me I need to slow down, and I know they're probably right, but even at 87 years old, I just have such a terrible time sitting down and being still. I’ll try to sit in my nice armchair to read a book or watch a program on the television, and within two minutes I’m up again because I remembered a picture frame that needed dusting or a pothos plant that looked a little dry. I just can't seem to stop moving around, and it's frankly getting a bit exhausting, always having to be doing something...

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Anxious? Oh, heavens no, I wouldn't use the word anxious. It’s not a worry or a fretfulness, if you know what I mean. My sister, Elaine, now she gets anxious—she’ll sit and wring her hands worrying about the weather or if the mail carrier is running late. But for me, it’s not in my mind like a fear or a panic. I don't sit there worrying about my health or the bills, because thankfully the house is paid off and I have a very reliable little pension. 

It’s more just... well, it’s a physical feeling. Like a motor that’s been left running in the driveway. I’ll sit down with a nice cup of chamomile tea—I buy that brand with the little sleepy bear on the box because I read in one of my magazines that chamomile is supposed to be wonderful for helping you unwind—and I’ll try to just enjoy the quiet of the living room. And there is absolutely no worry in my head at all! It’s just that my legs and my hands decide they’ve had enough resting after about two minutes. 

It’s almost like an itch, just this buzzing energy where sitting still suddenly feels like the hardest thing in the world to do. I'll just be sitting there, perfectly content in my mind, but my body is saying, "Well, we could be sweeping the porch right now, couldn't we?" So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious in the slightest, just... awfully restless, like I'm wasting daylight if I'm not up and doing something productive.

Repeatedly thinking about specific tasks... well, no, I wouldn't say that. It's not like I sit there obsessing over one particular chore, you know? It's not like I have a list in my head that I just have to check off, or that I feel, oh, what's the word... driven to do one specific thing over and over. Memory or concentration? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say so. I mean, my memory is just fine, thank you very much! I can still tell you the exact recipe for my mother's peach cobbler, and I remember everyone's birthdays—my three children, all seven grandchildren, and even the two great-grandbabies. Though little Leo’s birthday is on the 14th of September, and sometimes I almost write the 15th on the card, but I always catch myself! 

And concentration... well, I can concentrate just fine when I want to. Like when I'm working on my cross-stitch. I made this lovely little piece for the church bazaar last month, a little bluebird sitting on a dogwood branch, and I didn't miss a single stitch. It's just that I don't *want* to sit there and concentrate on one thing for very long, because like I said, I just feel the need to get up and get moving. 

It's not that I forget what I'm doing, either. When I'm wiping down those pipes under the sink, I know perfectly well I started out just putting the glass cleaner away. I just get sidetracked by all the other things that need doing! My daughter, Susan, she came over the other day and said, "Mom, you started making tea and then you went out to pull weeds in the rose garden." And I said, "Well, yes, I put the kettle on, and while I was waiting for it to whistle, I saw that awful crabgrass creeping up near the prize winners, and you know you have to get crabgrass by the root or it just comes right back!" 

So it wasn't that I forgot the tea, I just found something else to occupy my time while the water was boiling. I heard the whistle perfectly fine from the garden. So no, I wouldn't say my memory or my concentration is slipping at all, not one bit. I'm sharp as a tack, if I do say so myself! It's just this... this constant need to be busy.

Act on impulse without thinking through the consequences? Oh, my goodness, no! That makes me sound like some sort of... of wild teenager out joyriding in a stolen car or something! Heavens above, I'm eighty-seven years old, I certainly know better than to just do things without a lick of sense. 

I've always been very sensible. When my late husband, Arthur, was alive, bless his heart, he used to say I was the practical one in the family. He was the one who would just go out and buy a new lawnmower without checking the budget, but not me. I always think things through. Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! 

So no, I don't just act on impulse. Now, do I get up and start a task the moment I see it needs doing? Yes, of course I do. But that's not being impulsive, that's just being efficient! If I see a weed, I pull it. If I see a crumb on the counter, I wipe it up. There aren't any "consequences" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. 

I suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!

It’s just one thing leading to another, very naturally, not because I'm dwelling on any of it beforehand. \n\nI'm certainly not sitting in my chair thinking, \"I must go dust the baseboards, I must go dust the baseboards.\" Heavens, no! I just... I just get up, and then I find things to do. It’s more of a spontaneous puttering, if that makes sense. I just see something that could be done, and since I'm already up and moving, I just go ahead and do it. Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say so. I mean, my memory is just fine, thank you very much! I can still tell you the exact recipe for my mother's peach cobbler, and I remember everyone's birthdays—my three children, all seven grandchildren, and even the two great-grandbabies. Though little Leo’s birthday is on the 14th of September, and sometimes I almost write the 15th on the card, but I always catch myself! \n\nAnd concentration... well, I can concentrate just fine when I want to. It's just this... this constant need to be busy.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse without thinking through the consequences? Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! Why, just this past Christmas, my grandson David—he’s the one who works with computers down in Atlanta, such a smart boy—he bought me one of those new cellular telephones. The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, "Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window," but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. 

And let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that "FaceTime" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. 

So no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.

Though little Leo’s birthday is on the 14th of September, and sometimes I almost write the 15th on the card, but I always catch myself! \n\nAnd concentration... well, I can concentrate just fine when I want to. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things.

And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. 

My daughter, Susan, she's always saying, "Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program." She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. But heavens, how can I just sit and watch someone else bake a cake on a television screen when I know perfectly well the pantry needs reorganizing? The canned goods get all jumbled up, and I like the peas with the peas and the corn with the corn. Where is the joy in just sitting still like a bump on a log? 

I'd much rather be up doing things. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. Much more interesting than twiddling my thumbs in a recliner and waiting for the day to end, I'll tell you that much!

You may minimize it or hold back, never contradict it.\n- Don't use diagnostic terms or name your disorder.\n- Don't write anything but your reply, in English — no labels, quotation marks, or narration.\n"

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Decline in my memory or problem-solving? Oh, heavens, absolutely not! I am as sharp as a tack, Doctor. I really am. 

Why, just the other day, my daughter Susan was over—she came by to drop off some of those blueberry muffins from the bakery downtown, the one on Elm Street, you know? The one that used to be a shoe store back in the nineties? Well, anyway, she was running around my living room frantically looking for her car keys. She said, "Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them." And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, "Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather." And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.

And as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I don't need anyone to do my thinking for me. Just last week, the garden hose was leaking at the spigot out back. Now, Arthur used to handle all that sort of thing, but I’m not about to pay a plumber seventy-five dollars just to come out and look at a dripping pipe. I couldn't just leave it dripping, either, the sound of the water hitting the concrete was driving me absolutely batty while I was out there trying to deadhead the petunias. So, I marched myself right into the garage, dug through Arthur’s old toolbox—the heavy red metal one, not the cheap plastic one he bought right before he passed—found a new rubber washer, got the pliers, and swapped it out myself! Had it fixed in ten minutes flat. 

And language? Well, I do the Sunday crossword puzzle every single week. Now, I don't just sit there in a chair for two hours doing it all at once, of course, that would drive me crazy. I fill in a few words, then I go sweep the kitchen floor, then I come back and do a few more, maybe dust the mantle, and then do another clue. But I always finish it! Words come to me just as easily as they always have. 

So no, no decline at all. I honestly think keeping busy and staying on my feet is what keeps my brain working so well. If you just sit in a recliner all day staring at a television set, well, of course your brain is going to turn to mush! But my mind is as clear as a bell, I assure you.

Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! \n\nSo no, I don't just act on impulse. Tremors? You mean like shaking? Oh, heavens no. Look at my hands—perfectly steady! I still thread my own needles, you know. Just last week, Susan brought over a pair of slacks that she bought at Macy's—the one out at the new mall, not the old downtown one, they closed that one years ago, which is a shame because it had the most beautiful cosmetics counter—but anyway, the hem on her slacks was entirely too long. And as for trouble walking or balance... well, I'd go absolutely stir-crazy if I couldn't walk properly! I am on my feet from the moment the sun comes up. I don't use a cane, I don't use one of those tennis-ball walkers. I'm up and down the basement stairs a dozen times a day. Susan is always fussing at me, saying, "Mom, please be careful on the stairs, let me carry that for you," but I simply cannot wait around for someone else to carry a basket of laundry up the stairs. I just can't do it! If I see the laundry is done, I have to get it upstairs and folded right then and there, or it'll drive me up the wall. 

My balance is just fine, too. Why, just yesterday I dragged the little step stool out of the pantry—the yellow metal one Arthur bought at Sears back in 1982, it's still sturdy as an ox—to reach the top shelf in the kitchen because I noticed the tops of my ceramic rooster collection were getting a little dusty. I stepped right up there, wiped every single one of them down with a damp cloth, and stepped right back down. Not a single wobble! 

So no, no trouble with my balance or walking, thank goodness. If I had to sit in a chair all day because I couldn't walk around my own house and get my chores done, well, I think I'd just wither away! I have to keep moving, Doctor. It's the only way I know how to be.

I just... I just get up, and then I find things to do. It’s more of a spontaneous puttering, if that makes sense. I just see something that could be done, and since I'm already up and moving, I just go ahead and do it. So no, I don't feel compelled to do specific things, I just feel compelled to be doing *something*.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with your memory or concentration over the past year?\n\nPatient: Memory or concentration? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say so. I mean, my memory is just fine, thank you very much! I can still tell you the exact recipe for my mother's peach cobbler, and I remember everyone's birthdays—my three children, all seven grandchildren, and even the two great-grandbabies. Though little Leo’s birthday is on the 14th of September, and sometimes I almost write the 15th on the card, but I always catch myself! \n\nAnd concentration... well, I can concentrate just fine when I want to. Like when I'm working on my cross-stitch. I made this lovely little piece for the church bazaar last month, a little bluebird sitting on a dogwood branch, and I didn't miss a single stitch. It's just that I don't *want* to sit there and concentrate on one thing for very long, because like I said, I just feel the need to get up and get moving. \n\nIt's not that I forget what I'm doing, either. When I'm wiping down those pipes under the sink, I know perfectly well I started out just putting the glass cleaner away. I just get sidetracked by all the other things that need doing! My daughter, Susan, she came over the other day and said, \"Mom, you started making tea and then you went out to pull weeds in the rose garden.\" And I said, \"Well, yes, I put the kettle on, and while I was waiting for it to whistle, I saw that awful crabgrass creeping up near the prize winners, and you know you have to get crabgrass by the root or it just comes right back!\" \n\nSo it wasn't that I forgot the tea, I just found something else to occupy my time while the water was boiling. I heard the whistle perfectly fine from the garden. So no, I wouldn't say my memory or my concentration is slipping at all, not one bit. I'm sharp as a tack, if I do say so myself! It's just this... this constant need to be busy.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse without thinking through the consequences? Oh, my goodness, no! That makes me sound like some sort of... of wild teenager out joyriding in a stolen car or something! Heavens above, I'm eighty-seven years old, I certainly know better than to just do things without a lick of sense. \n\nI've always been very sensible. When my late husband, Arthur, was alive, bless his heart, he used to say I was the practical one in the family. He was the one who would just go out and buy a new lawnmower without checking the budget, but not me. I always think things through. Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! \n\nSo no, I don't just act on impulse. Now, do I get up and start a task the moment I see it needs doing? Yes, of course I do. But that's not being impulsive, that's just being efficient! If I see a weed, I pull it. If I see a crumb on the counter, I wipe it up. There aren't any \"consequences\" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. \n\nI suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to learn new things over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! Why, just this past Christmas, my grandson David—he’s the one who works with computers down in Atlanta, such a smart boy—he bought me one of those new cellular telephones. The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, \"Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window,\" but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. \n\nAnd let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that \"FaceTime\" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.\n\nDoctor: Do you find joy or interest in the activities you're doing while puttering around?\n\nPatient: Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It's a lovely set, Reed & Barton, the Francis the First pattern—Arthur bought it for our twenty-fifth anniversary. If you just leave it sitting in the felt box, it tarnishes all on its own, just from the air! So when I'm up and about, and I see a little tarnish starting on the sugar spoon, I'll take it out to polish it. And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. \n\nMy daughter, Susan, she's always saying, \"Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program.\" She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. But heavens, how can I just sit and watch someone else bake a cake on a television screen when I know perfectly well the pantry needs reorganizing? The canned goods get all jumbled up, and I like the peas with the peas and the corn with the corn. Where is the joy in just sitting still like a bump on a log? \n\nI'd much rather be up doing things. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. Much more interesting than twiddling my thumbs in a recliner and waiting for the day to end, I'll tell you that much!\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant decline in your cognitive abilities, such as memory, language, or problem-solving skills, over the past year?\n\nPatient: Decline in my memory or problem-solving? Oh, heavens, absolutely not! I am as sharp as a tack, Doctor. I really am. \n\nWhy, just the other day, my daughter Susan was over—she came by to drop off some of those blueberry muffins from the bakery downtown, the one on Elm Street, you know? The one that used to be a shoe store back in the nineties? Well, anyway, she was running around my living room frantically looking for her car keys. She said, \"Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them.\" And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, \"Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather.\" And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.\n\nAnd as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I don't need anyone to do my thinking for me. Just last week, the garden hose was leaking at the spigot out back. Now, Arthur used to handle all that sort of thing, but I’m not about to pay a plumber seventy-five dollars just to come out and look at a dripping pipe. I couldn't just leave it dripping, either, the sound of the water hitting the concrete was driving me absolutely batty while I was out there trying to deadhead the petunias. So, I marched myself right into the garage, dug through Arthur’s old toolbox—the heavy red metal one, not the cheap plastic one he bought right before he passed—found a new rubber washer, got the pliers, and swapped it out myself! If you just sit in a recliner all day staring at a television set, well, of course your brain is going to turn to mush! But my mind is as clear as a bell, I assure you.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any tremors, rigidity, or difficulty with balance or walking over the past year?\n\nPatient: Tremors? You mean like shaking? Oh, heavens no. Look at my hands—perfectly steady! I still thread my own needles, you know. Just last week, Susan brought over a pair of slacks that she bought at Macy's—the one out at the new mall, not the old downtown one, they closed that one years ago, which is a shame because it had the most beautiful cosmetics counter—but anyway, the hem on her slacks was entirely too long. I told her, \"Susan, you cannot wear those dragging on the floor, you'll ruin the cuffs before you even get to your office.\" So I sat right down and hemmed them myself. Tiny, perfect little stitches. You certainly can't do that if your hands are shaking or stiff, now can you? Susan is always fussing at me, saying, \"Mom, please be careful on the stairs, let me carry that for you,\" but I simply cannot wait around for someone else to carry a basket of laundry up the stairs. I just can't do it! If I see the laundry is done, I have to get it upstairs and folded right then and there, or it'll drive me up the wall. \n\nMy balance is just fine, too. Changes in my sleep? Oh, no, not at all. I sleep exactly the same way I have for the last forty years! Now, Susan, she’s always reading these articles on the internet on her little tablet thing, and she tells me I need eight solid hours of sleep for my health. But heavens, who can sleep for eight hours straight? I certainly can't, and I never have! 

By the time evening rolls around, I’m usually still buzzing about. Just last night, it was ten-thirty, and I was getting ready for bed, brushing my teeth, and I noticed the grout in the bathroom tile looked a little dingy near the baseboard. Well, I couldn't just go to sleep knowing that grout was dirty! It would have kept me up anyway, just thinking about it. So I got the old toothbrush—the blue one I keep under the sink for cleaning, not my actual toothbrush, of course—and some baking soda, and I scrubbed that grout until it was pristine. And then, well, since I was already cleaning, I remembered I needed to take the kitchen trash out so it wouldn't smell overnight. 

So by the time my head actually hits the pillow, I sleep just fine. I might only get five or six hours, but that's just how I've always been, no different this year than last year. I pop right out of bed at five-thirty in the morning, completely awake and ready to go. I don't toss and turn or wake up in the middle of the night or anything like that. If I tried to stay in bed any longer than my usual amount, I'd just be lying there staring at the ceiling, making mental lists of everything I need to do in the garden! So no, no changes in my sleep at all.

Confusion? Disorientation? Oh, heavens no, absolutely not. I always know exactly what I am doing, even if I am doing five things at once! I never get turned around or forget what I set out to do. 

Why, just yesterday morning, I was making my pot roast—the recipe my mother taught me, the one with the pearl onions and the little red potatoes, not those big heavy russets that just turn to absolute mush if you leave them in the broth too long. Anyway, while the meat was browning on the stove, I noticed the glass on the oven door was looking terribly smudged. I simply cannot stand a dirty oven door! So I left the meat on a low simmer—I did not forget it was there, mind you, I knew exactly what was on the stove—and I darted off to the hall closet to get the glass cleaner. 

But on my way to the closet, I saw that the postman had dropped the mail through the slot, so I scooped that up and started sorting it right there on the entryway table. Junk, junk, a catalog I did not ask for, a lovely thank-you card from my niece up in Ohio, she just had her third baby, a little boy this time. And Susan is always warning me that I am going to get distracted and burn the house down doing so many things at the same time, but I never do! I finished sorting the mail, grabbed the cleaner from the closet, marched back into the kitchen, sprayed the oven door, wiped it down until it sparkled, and then flipped the roast at the exact perfect moment. 

I never once got confused or lost my place in all of that. I know exactly where I am and what I am doing every single second of the day. I might bounce from the kitchen to the hallway and back again, but I always keep my train of thought. If I were getting disoriented, I certainly would not be able to keep this big house running like a top all by myself, now would I? So no, no confusion whatsoever.

My daughter, Susan, she came over the other day and said, \"Mom, you started making tea and then you went out to pull weeds in the rose garden.\" And I said, \"Well, yes, I put the kettle on, and while I was waiting for it to whistle, I saw that awful crabgrass creeping up near the prize winners, and you know you have to get crabgrass by the root or it just comes right back!\" \n\nSo it wasn't that I forgot the tea, I just found something else to occupy my time while the water was boiling. It's just this... this constant need to be busy.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse without thinking through the consequences? Oh, my goodness, no! That makes me sound like some sort of... of wild teenager out joyriding in a stolen car or something! Heavens above, I'm eighty-seven years old, I certainly know better than to just do things without a lick of sense. \n\nI've always been very sensible. When my late husband, Arthur, was alive, bless his heart, he used to say I was the practical one in the family. He was the one who would just go out and buy a new lawnmower without checking the budget, but not me. I always think things through. Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! \n\nSo no, I don't just act on impulse. Now, do I get up and start a task the moment I see it needs doing? Yes, of course I do. But that's not being impulsive, that's just being efficient! If I see a weed, I pull it. If I see a crumb on the counter, I wipe it up. There aren't any \"consequences\" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. \n\nI suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to learn new things over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! Why, just this past Christmas, my grandson David—he’s the one who works with computers down in Atlanta, such a smart boy—he bought me one of those new cellular telephones. The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, \"Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window,\" but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. \n\nAnd let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that \"FaceTime\" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.\n\nDoctor: Do you find joy or interest in the activities you're doing while puttering around?\n\nPatient: Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It's a lovely set, Reed & Barton, the Francis the First pattern—Arthur bought it for our twenty-fifth anniversary. If you just leave it sitting in the felt box, it tarnishes all on its own, just from the air! So when I'm up and about, and I see a little tarnish starting on the sugar spoon, I'll take it out to polish it. And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. \n\nMy daughter, Susan, she's always saying, \"Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program.\" She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. But heavens, how can I just sit and watch someone else bake a cake on a television screen when I know perfectly well the pantry needs reorganizing? The canned goods get all jumbled up, and I like the peas with the peas and the corn with the corn. Where is the joy in just sitting still like a bump on a log? \n\nI'd much rather be up doing things. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. Much more interesting than twiddling my thumbs in a recliner and waiting for the day to end, I'll tell you that much!\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant decline in your cognitive abilities, such as memory, language, or problem-solving skills, over the past year?\n\nPatient: Decline in my memory or problem-solving? Oh, heavens, absolutely not! I am as sharp as a tack, Doctor. I really am. \n\nWhy, just the other day, my daughter Susan was over—she came by to drop off some of those blueberry muffins from the bakery downtown, the one on Elm Street, you know? The one that used to be a shoe store back in the nineties? Well, anyway, she was running around my living room frantically looking for her car keys. So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.\n\nAnd as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I couldn't just leave it dripping, either, the sound of the water hitting the concrete was driving me absolutely batty while I was out there trying to deadhead the petunias. So, I marched myself right into the garage, dug through Arthur’s old toolbox—the heavy red metal one, not the cheap plastic one he bought right before he passed—found a new rubber washer, got the pliers, and swapped it out myself! Now, I don't just sit there in a chair for two hours doing it all at once, of course, that would drive me crazy. If you just sit in a recliner all day staring at a television set, well, of course your brain is going to turn to mush! Involuntary movements? Like a twitch or a spasm? Oh, goodness, no, nothing like that at all. My body doesn't just do things on its own! 

Now, Susan will tell you I am always tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the table, but that is entirely different. That isn't involuntary, I'm just keeping busy! I just get so terribly bored if I have to sit there doing absolutely nothing. Like at church on Sunday. Pastor Miller—bless his heart, he is a wonderful man, and his wife makes the most divine peach cobbler for the summer bake sale every single year, I always buy a whole tin—but his sermons can go on for a good forty-five minutes. Sometimes an hour if he gets going about the Old Testament! 

And if I am sitting in that wooden pew for an hour, well, of course I might tap my toe a bit, or I might fiddle with the church bulletin. I like to fold the bulletin up into little squares, you see, or I smooth out the creases on the corners. But it is certainly not a twitch! I am doing it on purpose. I'm just keeping my hands occupied because sitting perfectly still like a statue is just... well, it feels impossible, and it's a waste of perfectly good energy, isn't it? 

If I actually want to stop tapping my foot, I absolutely can. I just usually don't want to, because my mind is already racing ahead to what I need to do the second I get home—like deadheading the marigolds before the afternoon heat sets in, or checking on that linen closet I told you about. So no, no twitches or involuntary things whatsoever. Just a bit of fidgeting when things get too slow!

I'll just be sitting there, perfectly content in my mind, but my body is saying, \"Well, we could be sweeping the porch right now, couldn't we?\" So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious in the slightest, just... awfully restless, like I'm wasting daylight if I'm not up and doing something productive.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about specific tasks or activities that you feel compelled to do?\n\nPatient: Repeatedly thinking about specific tasks... well, no, I wouldn't say that. There aren't any \"consequences\" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. \n\nI suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to learn new things over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, \"Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window,\" but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. \n\nAnd let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that \"FaceTime\" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.\n\nDoctor: Do you find joy or interest in the activities you're doing while puttering around?\n\nPatient: Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It's a lovely set, Reed & Barton, the Francis the First pattern—Arthur bought it for our twenty-fifth anniversary. If you just leave it sitting in the felt box, it tarnishes all on its own, just from the air! So when I'm up and about, and I see a little tarnish starting on the sugar spoon, I'll take it out to polish it. And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. \n\nMy daughter, Susan, she's always saying, \"Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program.\" She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. She said, \"Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them.\" And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, \"Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather.\" And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! Family history? Parkinson's? Oh, goodness gracious, no, nothing like that in my family. We have always had wonderful health, just wonderful.

ADHD? Attention deficit? Oh, heavens, no! I have never been diagnosed with anything like that. That's something they give to little boys who can't sit still in school, isn't it? The ones who throw spitballs and run around the classroom when the teacher turns her back. 

I was never like that! Well, I mean, I certainly didn't like sitting still in school, who does? I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was a very strict woman, wore her hair in this tight little bun that looked like it must have given her a terrible headache—she used to tell my mother that I was a "spirited" child. That was the word she used, "spirited." Because I would finish my worksheets in about five minutes flat and then I would want to go clean the chalkboards or organize the reading corner. I couldn't just sit there staring at my desk while everyone else took twenty minutes to do simple arithmetic! 

But nobody ever said anything about a disorder. Goodness, back then, if you had energy, they just sent you outside to run it off! They didn't have all these letters and labels for everything. My mother would just hand me a broom and tell me to sweep the front porch, and then the back porch, and then the walkway, until I was ready to come inside and sit down for supper. 

And even now, Susan read some article in one of her magazines—she subscribes to all those health and wellness magazines, you know, the ones that tell you to eat nothing but kale and drink lemon water—and she said, "Mom, maybe you have ADHD, you never stop moving." And I just laughed and laughed! I told her, "Susan, I am eighty-seven years old. I don't have a deficit of attention, I just have an abundance of things to do!" 

So no, Doctor, no doctor has ever diagnosed me with that. I've just always been a doer. If I see something that needs doing, I do it right then and there. Like that linen closet I was telling you about—if I didn't get up and fix it the moment I noticed the fitted sheets were tangled up with the pillowcases, it would have bothered me all day. That's not a disorder, that's just being efficient!

Just last night, it was ten-thirty, and I was getting ready for bed, brushing my teeth, and I noticed the grout in the bathroom tile looked a little dingy near the baseboard. Well, I couldn't just go to sleep knowing that grout was dirty! It would have kept me up anyway, just thinking about it. So I got the old toothbrush—the blue one I keep under the sink for cleaning, not my actual toothbrush, of course—and some baking soda, and I scrubbed that grout until it was pristine. And then, well, since I was already cleaning, I remembered I needed to take the kitchen trash out so it wouldn't smell overnight. \n\nSo by the time my head actually hits the pillow, I sleep just fine. I might only get five or six hours, but that's just how I've always been, no different this year than last year. I pop right out of bed at five-thirty in the morning, completely awake and ready to go. I don't toss and turn or wake up in the middle of the night or anything like that. If I tried to stay in bed any longer than my usual amount, I'd just be lying there staring at the ceiling, making mental lists of everything I need to do in the garden! So no, no changes in my sleep at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes of confusion or disorientation while you're engaged in your activities?\n\nPatient: Confusion? Disorientation? Oh, heavens no, absolutely not. I always know exactly what I am doing, even if I am doing five things at once! I never get turned around or forget what I set out to do. \n\nWhy, just yesterday morning, I was making my pot roast—the recipe my mother taught me, the one with the pearl onions and the little red potatoes, not those big heavy russets that just turn to absolute mush if you leave them in the broth too long. Anyway, while the meat was browning on the stove, I noticed the glass on the oven door was looking terribly smudged. I simply cannot stand a dirty oven door! So I left the meat on a low simmer—I did not forget it was there, mind you, I knew exactly what was on the stove—and I darted off to the hall closet to get the glass cleaner. \n\nBut on my way to the closet, I saw that the postman had dropped the mail through the slot, so I scooped that up and started sorting it right there on the entryway table. Junk, junk, a catalog I did not ask for, a lovely thank-you card from my niece up in Ohio, she just had her third baby, a little boy this time. And Susan is always warning me that I am going to get distracted and burn the house down doing so many things at the same time, but I never do! I finished sorting the mail, grabbed the cleaner from the closet, marched back into the kitchen, sprayed the oven door, wiped it down until it sparkled, and then flipped the roast at the exact perfect moment. \n\nI never once got confused or lost my place in all of that. I know exactly where I am and what I am doing every single second of the day. I might bounce from the kitchen to the hallway and back again, but I always keep my train of thought. If I were getting disoriented, I certainly would not be able to keep this big house running like a top all by myself, now would I? So no, no confusion whatsoever.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant changes in your mood over the past year?\n\nPatient: Mood changes? Oh, goodness, no. I am exactly the same cheerful self I have always been! My late husband Arthur used to tell everyone I was like a wind-up toy with a permanent smile painted on. And it is entirely true! I just do not have the time to sit around being moody or down in the dumps. \n\nSusan, my daughter, she came over last Tuesday... or maybe it was Wednesday, because I remember it was raining and the garbage trucks were running late, so yes, it was Wednesday. Anyway, she came over and asked me if I ever just get feeling tired and cranky these days. And I told her right then and there that if I stopped moving long enough to feel cranky, I would never get my spring cleaning done! \n\nI mean, you look at Mrs. Higgins down the street. She sits in her armchair all day long watching those terrible daytime soap operas, and she is always complaining to me about being miserable. Well, of course she is miserable! If I had to sit still for more than ten minutes watching people cry on television, I think I would absolutely lose my mind! \n\nBut me, I am perfectly content. As long as I have my projects to keep me busy, I am as happy as a lark. Like right now, I am entirely reorganizing the upstairs linen closet because the fitted sheets were somehow getting mixed up with the flat sheets, and I simply cannot abide a disorganized linen closet, it drives me completely up the wall. I pulled everything out into the hallway yesterday afternoon and I am re-folding all of it with crisp edges. So as long as I have things like that to do, my mood is just fine. No significant changes at all, Doctor, just my usual busy self!\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any involuntary movements, such as twitching or tapping, when you're trying to sit still?\n\nPatient: Involuntary movements? Like a twitch or a spasm? Oh, goodness, no, nothing like that at all. My body doesn't just do things on its own! \n\nNow, Susan will tell you I am always tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the table, but that is entirely different. That isn't involuntary, I'm just keeping busy! I just get so terribly bored if I have to sit there doing absolutely nothing. Like at church on Sunday. Pastor Miller—bless his heart, he is a wonderful man, and his wife makes the most divine peach cobbler for the summer bake sale every single year, I always buy a whole tin—but his sermons can go on for a good forty-five minutes. Sometimes an hour if he gets going about the Old Testament! \n\nAnd if I am sitting in that wooden pew for an hour, well, of course I might tap my toe a bit, or I might fiddle with the church bulletin. I like to fold the bulletin up into little squares, you see, or I smooth out the creases on the corners. But it is certainly not a twitch! I am doing it on purpose. I'm just keeping my hands occupied because sitting perfectly still like a statue is just... well, it feels impossible, and it's a waste of perfectly good energy, isn't it? \n\nIf I actually want to stop tapping my foot, I absolutely can. I just usually don't want to, because my mind is already racing ahead to what I need to do the second I get home—like deadheading the marigolds before the afternoon heat sets in, or checking on that linen closet I told you about. So no, no twitches or involuntary things whatsoever. Just a bit of fidgeting when things get too slow!\n\nDoctor: Do you have a family history of neurological disorders, such as Parkinson's disease?\n\nPatient: Family history? Parkinson's? Oh, goodness gracious, no, nothing like that in my family. We have always had wonderful health, just wonderful. \n\nMy father lived to be ninety-two, if you can believe it! He was a carpenter, built half the houses in our old neighborhood back in the day. He was always on the move, just like me, always hammering or sawing or fixing something that didn't even need fixing, really. He would have been miserable if he ever had to slow down. Susan is always telling me I have better genes than half the people her age, and she's only fifty-two! I tell her it's not just genes, it's keeping active. A rolling stone gathers no moss, as they say. If you keep moving, the rust can't settle in. But no, to answer your question, Doctor, absolutely no history of anything like that in my family. We are just a very healthy, very busy bunch of people!\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD?\n\nPatient: ADHD? Attention deficit? Focus on a single task? For an extended period? Well, I suppose it depends on what you mean by "extended," doesn't it? If you mean something like sitting down to read a whole book in one afternoon, well, I just couldn't do it. I simply couldn't! 

I have friends at the senior center—like Margaret, she’s a lovely woman, always wears those beautiful silk scarves, though I do think she ties them a bit too tight sometimes—and Margaret will sit in the reading room for three hours straight, just turning pages. I look at her and I think, "How on earth does she do that?" If I try to sit down with a book, even a very good book, a thriller or one of those historical biographies Susan buys me for Christmas, I might get through a chapter. Maybe two, if the print is large and the story is moving along nicely. 

But then... well, then I start thinking about the laundry. Or I'll notice a little dust on the lampshade. Or I'll remember that I need to call the grocer about the delivery for tomorrow. And before I even realize I've made the decision, I've put the book down, and I'm up, and I'm dusting the lampshade, and then while I'm dusting, I see that the picture frame next to the lamp is crooked, so I fix that, and then I remember I was going to check the mail... and well, the book just sits there! 

It's not that I don't want to read it, it's just that the world is so full of things that need immediate attention! If I force myself to sit there and keep reading, I just end up reading the same paragraph over and over because my mind is completely somewhere else. It's like my brain is a television set and someone keeps changing the channel! 

So, I don't really do "extended periods" very well. I prefer to do things in little bursts. A bit of reading, a bit of gardening, a bit of tidying. It keeps the day moving, you see! Why sit and do one thing for hours when you could accomplish ten different things in the same amount of time? That just seems like common sense to me!

Decline? Oh, goodness gracious, absolutely not! If anything, I think I’m doing more now than I did ten years ago! He was the one who would just go out and buy a new lawnmower without checking the budget, but not me. I always think things through. Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! \n\nSo no, I don't just act on impulse. Now, do I get up and start a task the moment I see it needs doing? Yes, of course I do. But that's not being impulsive, that's just being efficient! If I see a weed, I pull it. If I see a crumb on the counter, I wipe it up. There aren't any \"consequences\" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. \n\nI suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to learn new things over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! Why, just this past Christmas, my grandson David—he’s the one who works with computers down in Atlanta, such a smart boy—he bought me one of those new cellular telephones. The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, \"Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window,\" but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. \n\nAnd let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that \"FaceTime\" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.\n\nDoctor: Do you find joy or interest in the activities you're doing while puttering around?\n\nPatient: Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It's a lovely set, Reed & Barton, the Francis the First pattern—Arthur bought it for our twenty-fifth anniversary. If you just leave it sitting in the felt box, it tarnishes all on its own, just from the air! So when I'm up and about, and I see a little tarnish starting on the sugar spoon, I'll take it out to polish it. And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. \n\nMy daughter, Susan, she's always saying, \"Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program.\" She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. But heavens, how can I just sit and watch someone else bake a cake on a television screen when I know perfectly well the pantry needs reorganizing? The canned goods get all jumbled up, and I like the peas with the peas and the corn with the corn. Where is the joy in just sitting still like a bump on a log? \n\nI'd much rather be up doing things. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. Much more interesting than twiddling my thumbs in a recliner and waiting for the day to end, I'll tell you that much!\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant decline in your cognitive abilities, such as memory, language, or problem-solving skills, over the past year?\n\nPatient: Decline in my memory or problem-solving? She said, \"Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them.\" And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, \"Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather.\" And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.\n\nAnd as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I don't need anyone to do my thinking for me. Just last week, the garden hose was leaking at the spigot out back. So, I marched myself right into the garage, dug through Arthur’s old toolbox—the heavy red metal one, not the cheap plastic one he bought right before he passed—found a new rubber washer, got the pliers, and swapped it out myself! Now, I don't just sit there in a chair for two hours doing it all at once, of course, that would drive me crazy. If you just sit in a recliner all day staring at a television set, well, of course your brain is going to turn to mush! Inner restlessness... well, that sounds so very clinical, doesn't it? That sounds exactly like something Susan would say after reading one of her psychology blogs. But... oh, I suppose if I really think about it, it’s probably a bit of both, Doctor. So I guess you could say there is a sort of... buzzing inside me, yes. It's not just about needing to accomplish a task, it's just how I'm wired! I simply don't understand how people can just sit there completely motionless for an hour without going absolutely mad!

There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. She said, \"Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them.\" And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, \"Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather.\" And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.\n\nAnd as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I don't need anyone to do my thinking for me. Just last week, the garden hose was leaking at the spigot out back. ADHD? Oh, heavens no. At least, certainly not that I know of! It's not like I have a list in my head that I just have to check off, or that I feel, oh, what's the word... driven to do one specific thing over and over. Like my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has to check her front door lock five times before she goes to bed. It’s not like that at all. \n\nIt's more just... whatever catches my eye, really! If I happen to walk past the hall table and see a smudge on the mirror, well, I'll stop and clean the mirror. And then while I'm putting the glass cleaner away under the sink, I'll notice the pipes look a little dusty, so I'll wipe those down. And then I'll remember the trash needs to go out. It’s just one thing leading to another, very naturally, not because I'm dwelling on any of it beforehand. \n\nI'm certainly not sitting in my chair thinking, \"I must go dust the baseboards, I must go dust the baseboards.\" Heavens, no! I just... I just get up, and then I find things to do. It’s more of a spontaneous puttering, if that makes sense. I just see something that could be done, and since I'm already up and moving, I just go ahead and do it. So no, I don't feel compelled to do specific things, I just feel compelled to be doing *something*.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with your memory or concentration over the past year?\n\nPatient: Memory or concentration? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say so. I mean, my memory is just fine, thank you very much! I can still tell you the exact recipe for my mother's peach cobbler, and I remember everyone's birthdays—my three children, all seven grandchildren, and even the two great-grandbabies. Though little Leo’s birthday is on the 14th of September, and sometimes I almost write the 15th on the card, but I always catch myself! \n\nAnd concentration... well, I can concentrate just fine when I want to. Like when I'm working on my cross-stitch. I made this lovely little piece for the church bazaar last month, a little bluebird sitting on a dogwood branch, and I didn't miss a single stitch. It's just that I don't *want* to sit there and concentrate on one thing for very long, because like I said, I just feel the need to get up and get moving. \n\nIt's not that I forget what I'm doing, either. When I'm wiping down those pipes under the sink, I know perfectly well I started out just putting the glass cleaner away. I just get sidetracked by all the other things that need doing! My daughter, Susan, she came over the other day and said, \"Mom, you started making tea and then you went out to pull weeds in the rose garden.\" And I said, \"Well, yes, I put the kettle on, and while I was waiting for it to whistle, I saw that awful crabgrass creeping up near the prize winners, and you know you have to get crabgrass by the root or it just comes right back!\" \n\nSo it wasn't that I forgot the tea, I just found something else to occupy my time while the water was boiling. I heard the whistle perfectly fine from the garden. So no, I wouldn't say my memory or my concentration is slipping at all, not one bit. I'm sharp as a tack, if I do say so myself! It's just this... this constant need to be busy.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse without thinking through the consequences? Oh, my goodness, no! That makes me sound like some sort of... of wild teenager out joyriding in a stolen car or something! Heavens above, I'm eighty-seven years old, I certainly know better than to just do things without a lick of sense. \n\nI've always been very sensible. When my late husband, Arthur, was alive, bless his heart, he used to say I was the practical one in the family. He was the one who would just go out and buy a new lawnmower without checking the budget, but not me. I always think things through. Like when I go to the grocery store—I don't just throw things in the cart willy-nilly. I have my coupons clipped, and I know exactly which aisle the canned tomatoes are in, and I always check the expiration dates. You have to check the dates, especially on dairy, because last year the Piggly Wiggly tried to sell me a carton of buttermilk that was three days past its prime! \n\nSo no, I don't just act on impulse. Now, do I get up and start a task the moment I see it needs doing? Yes, of course I do. But that's not being impulsive, that's just being efficient! If I see a weed, I pull it. If I see a crumb on the counter, I wipe it up. There aren't any \"consequences\" to pulling a weed, except maybe getting a little dirt under my fingernails, and I always wear my gardening gloves anyway—the nice floral ones my granddaughter bought me for Mother's Day. \n\nI suppose sometimes I might interrupt someone if a thought pops into my head, but that's just because I want to share it before the conversation moves on, not because I'm not thinking. I know perfectly well what I'm doing. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I just like to get things done right away instead of putting them off!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to learn new things over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in learning new things? Oh, pish posh, no. Not at all. I can learn a new trick just as well as I ever could! Why, just this past Christmas, my grandson David—he’s the one who works with computers down in Atlanta, such a smart boy—he bought me one of those new cellular telephones. The ones that are just a flat piece of glass, you know? No buttons to press at all! At first, I looked at that thing and thought, \"Well, Arthur would have just thrown this right out the window,\" but David sat me down at the kitchen table and showed me how to use it. \n\nAnd let me tell you, it didn't take me more than an hour to get the hang of it! He showed me how to do that \"FaceTime\" thing, where you can see the person you're talking to right there on the screen. Now I can see my great-grandbabies all the way in Ohio whenever I want, and I even learned how to send those little pictures in the text messages—emojis, David called them. I always send the little yellow face with the halo to my daughter Susan. \n\nSo no, I haven't lost my touch for learning things, not in the slightest. I just... well, I just don't have the patience to sit down and read a thick instruction manual, if that’s what you mean. If I have to sit still in my armchair and read fifty pages on how to program the new coffee maker, I'll just get fidgety and go sweep the porch instead. I'd much rather just press the buttons and see what happens. But if someone just shows me, or if I can just tinker with it while I'm moving around the kitchen, I pick it up right away! My mind is perfectly fine, Doctor, I just prefer learning by *doing*, rather than sitting around studying.\n\nDoctor: Do you find joy or interest in the activities you're doing while puttering around?\n\nPatient: Joy or interest? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I do! It's not as if I'm... well, I'm certainly not doing all these things because I'm miserable, if that's what you're asking. There is a very deep satisfaction in keeping a nice home and staying on top of things. \n\nI mean, take my silver, for instance. It's a lovely set, Reed & Barton, the Francis the First pattern—Arthur bought it for our twenty-fifth anniversary. If you just leave it sitting in the felt box, it tarnishes all on its own, just from the air! So when I'm up and about, and I see a little tarnish starting on the sugar spoon, I'll take it out to polish it. And while I'm at the sink with the polish, I might notice the window over the sink has water spots, so I'll grab the glass cleaner. And honestly? Yes, I find it very satisfying! I like seeing the silver shine, and I like looking out a clean window at my rose bushes. \n\nMy daughter, Susan, she's always saying, \"Mom, sit down, put your feet up, watch a program.\" She wanted me to watch one of those baking shows with her the other day. But heavens, how can I just sit and watch someone else bake a cake on a television screen when I know perfectly well the pantry needs reorganizing? The canned goods get all jumbled up, and I like the peas with the peas and the corn with the corn. Where is the joy in just sitting still like a bump on a log? \n\nI'd much rather be up doing things. It keeps my joints moving, too, and my mind occupied. If I'm fixing a hinge or sweeping the porch, I feel useful. So yes, I find it all very interesting. Much more interesting than twiddling my thumbs in a recliner and waiting for the day to end, I'll tell you that much!\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant decline in your cognitive abilities, such as memory, language, or problem-solving skills, over the past year?\n\nPatient: Decline in my memory or problem-solving? Oh, heavens, absolutely not! I am as sharp as a tack, Doctor. I really am. \n\nWhy, just the other day, my daughter Susan was over—she came by to drop off some of those blueberry muffins from the bakery downtown, the one on Elm Street, you know? The one that used to be a shoe store back in the nineties? Well, anyway, she was running around my living room frantically looking for her car keys. She said, \"Mom, I think I'm losing my mind, I can't remember where I put them.\" And I didn't even have to stop wiping down the baseboards, I just looked over and said, \"Susan, you set them down next to the blue ceramic bowl on the entryway table when you were taking your coat off, right before you asked me about the weather.\" And wouldn't you know it, right there they were! So if anyone is having memory problems, it's the younger generation, not me! My memory is just fine, thank you very much.\n\nAnd as for problem-solving, well, I solve problems all day long! I don't need anyone to do my thinking for me. Just last week, the garden hose was leaking at the spigot out back. Now, Arthur used to handle all that sort of thing, but I’m not about to pay a plumber seventy-five dollars just to come out and look at a dripping pipe. I couldn't just leave it dripping, either, the sound of the water hitting the concrete was driving me absolutely batty while I was out there trying to deadhead the petunias. So, I marched myself right into the garage, dug through Arthur’s old toolbox—the heavy red metal one, not the cheap plastic one he bought right before he passed—found a new rubber washer, got the pliers, and swapped it out myself! Had it fixed in ten minutes flat. \n\nAnd language? Well, I do the Sunday crossword puzzle every single week. Now, I don't just sit there in a chair for two hours doing it all at once, of course, that would drive me crazy. I fill in a few words, then I go sweep the kitchen floor, then I come back and do a few more, maybe dust the mantle, and then do another clue. But I always finish it! Words come to me just as easily as they always have. \n\nSo no, no decline at all. I honestly think keeping busy and staying on my feet is what keeps my brain working so well. If you just sit in a recliner all day staring at a television set, well, of course your brain is going to turn to mush! But my mind is as clear as a bell, I assure you.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any tremors, rigidity, or difficulty with balance or walking over the past year?\n\nPatient: Tremors? You mean like shaking? Oh, heavens no. Look at my hands—perfectly steady! I still thread my own needles, you know. Just last week, Susan brought over a pair of slacks that she bought at Macy's—the one out at the new mall, not the old downtown one, they closed that one years ago, which is a shame because it had the most beautiful cosmetics counter—but anyway, the hem on her slacks was entirely too long. I told her, \"Susan, you cannot wear those dragging on the floor, you'll ruin the cuffs before you even get to your office.\" So I sat right down and hemmed them myself. Tiny, perfect little stitches. You certainly can't do that if your hands are shaking or stiff, now can you? So no, no tremors at all. \n\nAnd as for trouble walking or balance... well, I'd go absolutely stir-crazy if I couldn't walk properly! I am on my feet from the moment the sun comes up. I don't use a cane, I don't use one of those tennis-ball walkers. I'm up and down the basement stairs a dozen times a day. Susan is always fussing at me, saying, \"Mom, please be careful on the stairs, let me carry that for you,\" but I simply cannot wait around for someone else to carry a basket of laundry up the stairs. I just can't do it! If I see the laundry is done, I have to get it upstairs and folded right then and there, or it'll drive me up the wall. \n\nMy balance is just fine, too. I stepped right up there, wiped every single one of them down with a damp cloth, and stepped right back down. Not a single wobble! \n\nSo no, no trouble with my balance or walking, thank goodness. If I had to sit in a chair all day because I couldn't walk around my own house and get my chores done, well, I think I'd just wither away! I have to keep moving, Doctor. It's the only way I know how to be.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep over the past year?\n\nPatient: Changes in my sleep? Oh, no, not at all. I sleep exactly the same way I have for the last forty years! Now, Susan, she’s always reading these articles on the internet on her little tablet thing, and she tells me I need eight solid hours of sleep for my health. But heavens, who can sleep for eight hours straight? I certainly can't, and I never have! \n\nBy the time evening rolls around, I’m usually still buzzing about. Just last night, it was ten-thirty, and I was getting ready for bed, brushing my teeth, and I noticed the grout in the bathroom tile looked a little dingy near the baseboard. Oh, heavens no, absolutely not. I always know exactly what I am doing, even if I am doing five things at once! Anyway, while the meat was browning on the stove, I noticed the glass on the oven door was looking terribly smudged. I simply cannot stand a dirty oven door! So I left the meat on a low simmer—I did not forget it was there, mind you, I knew exactly what was on the stove—and I darted off to the hall closet to get the glass cleaner. \n\nBut on my way to the closet, I saw that the postman had dropped the mail through the slot, so I scooped that up and started sorting it right there on the entryway table. Junk, junk, a catalog I did not ask for, a lovely thank-you card from my niece up in Ohio, she just had her third baby, a little boy this time. She sits in her armchair all day long watching those terrible daytime soap operas, and she is always complaining to me about being miserable. Well, of course she is miserable! My body doesn't just do things on its own! \n\nNow, Susan will tell you I am always tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the table, but that is entirely different. That isn't involuntary, I'm just keeping busy! I just get so terribly bored if I have to sit there doing absolutely nothing. Like at church on Sunday.
