Just a bit of fidgeting when things get too slow!\n\nDoctor: Do you have a family history of neurological disorders, such as Parkinson's disease?\n\nPatient: Family history? Parkinson's? Oh, goodness gracious, no, nothing like that in my family. We have always had wonderful health, just wonderful. \n\nMy father lived to be ninety-two, if you can believe it! He was a carpenter, built half the houses in our old neighborhood back in the day. He was always on the move, just like me, always hammering or sawing or fixing something that didn't even need fixing, really. He would have been miserable if he ever had to slow down. But he never did! He was sharp as a tack right up until the end, and his hands were as steady as a rock. Never a shake or a tremor. \n\nAnd my mother, well, she made it to eighty-nine. She was a seamstress, made the most beautiful wedding gowns. You need a terribly steady hand for that kind of delicate beadwork, you know. She would sit by the window for the good light and sew for hours. I used to watch her when I was a little girl and think how I could never sit that still for that long, but she loved it. And she never had any sort of neurological... whatever you called it. No Parkinson's, no Alzheimer's, none of that business. \n\nI suppose we're just built sturdy! Susan is always telling me I have better genes than half the people her age, and she's only fifty-two! I tell her it's not just genes, it's keeping active. A rolling stone gathers no moss, as they say. If you keep moving, the rust can't settle in. But no, to answer your question, Doctor, absolutely no history of anything like that in my family. We are just a very healthy, very busy bunch of people!\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD?\n\nPatient: ADHD? Attention deficit? Oh, heavens, no! I have never been diagnosed with anything like that. That's something they give to little boys who can't sit still in school, isn't it? The ones who throw spitballs and run around the classroom when the teacher turns her back. \n\nI was never like that! Well, I mean, I certainly didn't like sitting still in school, who does? I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was a very strict woman, wore her hair in this tight little bun that looked like it must have given her a terrible headache—she used to tell my mother that I was a \"spirited\" child. That was the word she used, \"spirited.\" Because I would finish my worksheets in about five minutes flat and then I would want to go clean the chalkboards or organize the reading corner. I couldn't just sit there staring at my desk while everyone else took twenty minutes to do simple arithmetic! \n\nBut nobody ever said anything about a disorder. Goodness, back then, if you had energy, they just sent you outside to run it off! They didn't have all these letters and labels for everything. My mother would just hand me a broom and tell me to sweep the front porch, and then the back porch, and then the walkway, until I was ready to come inside and sit down for supper. \n\nAnd even now, Susan read some article in one of her magazines—she subscribes to all those health and wellness magazines, you know, the ones that tell you to eat nothing but kale and drink lemon water—and she said, \"Mom, maybe you have ADHD, you never stop moving.\" And I just laughed and laughed! Like that linen closet I was telling you about—if I didn't get up and fix it the moment I noticed the fitted sheets were tangled up with the pillowcases, it would have bothered me all day. That's not a disorder, that's just being efficient!\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what happens when you try to focus on a single task for an extended period of time?\n\nPatient: Focus on a single task? For an extended period? Well, I suppose it depends on what you mean by \"extended,\" doesn't it? If you mean something like sitting down to read a whole book in one afternoon, well, I just couldn't do it. I simply couldn't! \n\nI have friends at the senior center—like Margaret, she’s a lovely woman, always wears those beautiful silk scarves, though I do think she ties them a bit too tight sometimes—and Margaret will sit in the reading room for three hours straight, just turning pages. I look at her and I think, \"How on earth does she do that?\" If I try to sit down with a book, even a very good book, a thriller or one of those historical biographies Susan buys me for Christmas, I might get through a chapter. Maybe two, if the print is large and the story is moving along nicely. \n\nBut then... well, then I start thinking about the laundry. Or I'll notice a little dust on the lampshade. Or I'll remember that I need to call the grocer about the delivery for tomorrow. And before I even realize I've made the decision, I've put the book down, and I'm up, and I'm dusting the lampshade, and then while I'm dusting, I see that the picture frame next to the lamp is crooked, so I fix that, and then I remember I was going to check the mail... and well, the book just sits there! \n\nIt's not that I don't want to read it, it's just that the world is so full of things that need immediate attention! If I force myself to sit there and keep reading, I just end up reading the same paragraph over and over because my mind is completely somewhere else. It's like my brain is a television set and someone keeps changing the channel! \n\nSo, I don't really do \"extended periods\" very well. I prefer to do things in little bursts. A bit of reading, a bit of gardening, a bit of tidying. It keeps the day moving, you see! Why sit and do one thing for hours when you could accomplish ten different things in the same amount of time? That just seems like common sense to me!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any decline in your ability to perform daily tasks on your own without assistance?\n\nPatient: Decline? Oh, goodness gracious, absolutely not! If anything, I think I’m doing more now than I did ten years ago! Susan—my daughter, you remember I mentioned her—she is always hovering, always saying, \"Mom, let me do the grocery shopping,\" or \"Mom, let me hire someone to clean the gutters.\" The gutters! Can you imagine? I told her, \"Susan, I have a perfectly good step stool in the garage and I know exactly how to use it.\" Well, she nearly had a fit about the step stool, started going on and on about balance and age and all that nonsense, but that’s beside the point. \n\nThe point is, I do all my own cooking, my own cleaning, my laundry... I don't need any help with any of it. Oh, and the gardening! You should see my hydrangeas this year, Doctor, they are just spectacular. The secret is coffee grounds, you know. You sprinkle them around the base of the plant, and the acidity makes the blooms the most magnificent shade of blue. Anyway, I’m out there every single morning by seven o'clock, pulling weeds, pruning the rose bushes, sweeping the patio. \n\nI just can’t stand the idea of sitting around waiting for someone else to do things for me when I am perfectly capable of doing them myself! Why, just yesterday, the mailman—lovely young man, always wears shorts even in November, I don't know how his knees don't completely freeze over—he offered to carry a rather large package up the front steps for me, and I just snatched it right out of his hands! I said, \"Thank you very much, young man, but my legs work just fine!\" \n\nSo, no, I haven't noticed any decline in my abilities whatsoever. I suppose I might be a tiny bit slower getting up from my knees when I'm weeding the flowerbeds, but once I’m up, I’m off like a shot! I manage my whole house top to bottom, all by myself, without a lick of assistance from anyone.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your need to constantly be doing something is related to your own inner restlessness or is it driven by external factors, such as the need to accomplish specific tasks?\n\nPatient: Inner restlessness... well, that sounds so very clinical, doesn't it? That sounds exactly like something Susan would say after reading one of her psychology blogs. But... oh, I suppose if I really think about it, it’s probably a bit of both, Doctor. I mean, yes, I love checking things off my list and keeping a tidy home, but even when there absolutely isn't a single chore to do, I still can't just sit there like a bump on a log! \n\nTake the senior center, for example. They have these monthly planning meetings, and the woman who runs them, Brenda—lovely woman, makes a wonderful potato salad, but she talks at an absolute snail's pace. A snail! She reads the minutes from the last meeting word for word, and I just... well, I get this awful ants-in-my-chair feeling. I just can't bear it! I have to shift my weight around, cross my legs, uncross them, adjust my cardigan. Eventually, I just have to stand up and go get a cup of coffee from the back table, even if it's that terrible instant decaf and I don't even want it, just to have an excuse to move my legs! \n\nAnd it’s the exact same thing on Sundays. Pastor Miller gives a beautiful sermon, truly he does, but then we get to the church announcements, and they just go on and on and on. The bake sale, the choir practice, the youth group car wash... I find myself grabbing the hymnals and straightening them all out in the pew rack, or I'll take out all those little donation envelopes and the tiny golf pencils and organize them into neat little stacks just to get through it! \n\nIf I don't give my hands something to do or move my body a little bit when things get slow, I feel like I'm going to burst right out of my own skin. So I guess you could say there is a sort of... buzzing inside me, yes. It's not just about needing to accomplish a task, it's just how I'm wired! I simply don't understand how people can just sit there completely motionless for an hour without going absolutely mad!\n\nDoctor: Do you have any family members who have been diagnosed with ADHD?\n\nPatient: ADHD? Oh, heavens no. At least, certainly not that I know of! You have to remember, Doctor, back when my siblings and I were growing up—this would have been the late thirties and early forties—nobody had all these alphabet soup diagnoses. If you were a child who couldn't sit still, you weren't given a medical label, you were just called \"spirited,\" or my mother would say you had \"ants in your pants\" and she'd send you out to run around the yard until you tired yourself out! \n\nMy older brother, Arthur—he passed away back in 2012, bless his heart, a terrible business with his gallbladder that just cascaded into all sorts of trouble, but that's neither here nor there—Arthur was exactly like me. He could not sit still to save his life! He was always tinkering with something. Everything has to be scheduled and color-coded on that electronic calendar on her telephone. She certainly doesn't have any trouble sitting at a desk for hours on end, though she does have trouble letting me do things my own way, as I've already told you! \n\nSo, no, no one in the family has ever been officially diagnosed with anything like that. But as far as a doctor actually writing down a diagnosis on a piece of paper? No, absolutely not. None of that in our family.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your restlessness and need to constantly be doing something might be related to how your brain is wired, rather than just a response to your environment?\n\nPatient: How my brain is wired? I try to read them, I really do, because she gets so huffy if I don't, but it just sounds like a lot of scientific mumbo jumbo to me. \n\nSo, is it my brain, or is it my environment? Well... Even when Harold and I—Harold was my late husband, passed in '98, wonderful man but he could sleep through an absolute hurricane—when we used to go to Florida for the winters, down in Boca, everyone else would be lounging by the pool with their little umbrella drinks, just baking in the sun for hours on end. And what was I doing? I was organizing the pool chairs! I was walking up and down the beach collecting seashells, sorting them by size and color on our little patio table until Harold would say, \"Martha, for heaven's sake, sit down and look at the ocean!\" But I was looking at the ocean, I just didn't see the need to be completely stationary while doing it! \n\nSo, if you're asking if it's just because my house is messy and I need to clean it, or because my environment is demanding things of me... well, I suppose not, because even on a vacation with absolutely zero chores, I'm still buzzing around like a bee in a bonnet. But is that because of my actual brain wiring? I truly don't know the first thing about how brains are wired. Maybe I'm just used to a lifetime of doing things! When you spend eighty-seven years keeping your hands busy and raising a family and keeping a home, I imagine your body just forgets how to stop. It's like a train that's built up too much steam, you know? You can't just throw the brakes on all at once. But as for the medical side of it, the wiring and the circuits and all that... you're the doctor, so you tell me, because I truly haven't got a clue!"
